question: When may a police officer arrest a person without a warrant?
answer_text: A police‑officer can arrest without a magistrate’s order or a warrant in two situations: (1) when a person commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence, and (2) when there is a reasonable complaint, credible information, or reasonable suspicion that a person has committed a cognizable offence punishable by imprisonment of up to seven years (with or without fine), provided the officer has reason to believe this on the basis of the complaint or information and the other conditions listed in the Code are satisfied.

question: How long may the police detain a person arrested without a warrant before producing him before a Magistrate?
answer_text: The police may keep a person arrested without a warrant in police custody for up to fifteen days before the person must be produced before a Magistrate; no magistrate can authorize police custody beyond that period.

question: Can the police investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order from a Magistrate?
answer_text: No. A police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable offence unless a Magistrate of the first or second class orders the investigation.

question: May an officer in charge of a police station investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate's order?
answer_text: Yes. An officer in charge of a police‑station is authorized to investigate a cognizable case without first obtaining an order from a Magistrate.

question: Can a police officer require a witness to attend before him during an investigation?
answer_text: Yes. A police officer conducting an investigation may, by a written order, require any person who is within his own or an adjoining station’s limits and appears to be acquainted with the case to attend before him, and that person must comply.

question: Is a witness bound to answer police questions whose answers would expose him to a criminal charge?
answer_text: No. A person examined by police is bound to answer all questions except those whose answers would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture.

question: Must a statement made to a police officer during investigation be signed by the person making it?

Section 164 says statements are to be recorded in any manner the officer thinks best fitted for the circumstances, and only confessions are required to be signed as provided in section 364. question: May a police officer offer an inducement or promise to obtain a statement?
answer_text: No. A police officer is prohibited from offering any inducement or promise to obtain a statement; they must not prevent a person from making a statement of his own free will.

question: Who may record a confession, and what must be explained to the person before recording it?
answer_text: Any Magistrate may record a confession. Before doing so, the Magistrate must explain to the person that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does, the confession may be used as evidence against him.

question: On what basis may a Magistrate take cognizance of an offence?
answer_text: A Magistrate may take cognizance of an offence when he receives a complaint of the facts constituting the offence, when he receives a written report of such facts from a police officer, when he receives information from any other person, or when he has his own knowledge or suspicion that the offence has been committed.

question: What must a Magistrate do on taking cognizance of an offence upon a complaint?
answer_text: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on a complaint, he must examine the complainant (and any witness, if any) as required by law.

question: When may a Magistrate postpone the issue of process against a person complained against?

question: What may a Magistrate do where an accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious?
answer_text: A Magistrate who believes an accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious may first call on the complainant (or, if absent, issue a summons) to show cause why he should not pay compensation to the accused. The Magistrate must record any cause shown and, if satisfied, may order compensation not exceeding fifty thousand Taka (or twenty‑five thousand Taka for a Magistrate of the third class) to be paid by the complainant to the accused. If the payment is not made, the Magistrate may also order simple imprisonment of the complainant for up to thirty days.

question: Who may tender a pardon to an accomplice, and in which cases?
answer_text: A pardon to an accomplice may be tendered by the Court of Session, or by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The tender is made when the person is believed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in, or privy to, the offence and the purpose is to obtain his evidence at trial.

question: Under what circumstances may an accused person be tried in his absence?
answer_text: An accused may be tried in his absence when it is proved that he has absconded and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, and his attendance cannot be obtained without an unreasonable amount of delay, expense or inconvenience. In such a case the court may, in his absence, examine the prosecution witnesses, record their depositions and use those depositions as evidence at the inquiry or trial.

question: Can an accused be punished for refusing to answer questions put to him by the court?
answer_text: No. Under the Code an accused person is not liable to punishment for refusing to answer questions put to him by the court; the court may only draw inferences from the refusal or the answers given.

question: Are criminal courts open to the public?
answer_text: Yes. By default the place where any criminal court sits for inquiry or trial is deemed an open court and the public generally may have access, subject to the judge or magistrate’s power to restrict access at any stage.

question: Can a person who has been acquitted be tried again for the same offence?
answer_text: No. Under Section 403 a person who has been acquitted may not be tried again for the same offence.

question: Who may present an appeal against an order of acquittal?
answer_text: An appeal against an order of acquittal may be presented either by the Government, which can direct the Public Prosecutor to file the appeal, or, in cases instituted upon a complaint where the order involves an error of law, by the complainant themselves.

question: What inherent power does the High Court Division retain under the Code?
answer_text: The High Court Division retains the inherent power to transfer cases and appeals (or to order a transfer) whenever it appears that such transfer will promote the ends of justice or the general convenience of parties or witnesses.
